title: Narada comes to Sanatkumara: "I know the Vedas — I don't know the Self" (7.1)
hook: the most learned sage in the room lists everything he has studied, then admits he is still in sorrow

segments.voice: Yesterday: Uddalaka's last lessons, the hot axe, and a son who finally understood. Your line was truth protects.

Every degree on the wall. Diplomas in three languages. A shelf of books with their name on the spine. People call for advice. And one night, the person who owns all of it sits across from a friend and says, quietly: I know all this, and I'm not okay. The seventh chapter of the Chandogya opens with that scene. The man with the diplomas is Narada, a famous sage, and the one he goes to is the sage Sanatkumara.
screen: `EVERY DEGREE ON THE WALL.` → `I KNOW ALL THIS.` → `AND I'M NOT OKAY.`

segments.voice: Teach me, sir, Narada says. Sanatkumara answers: first tell me what you already know, and I'll teach you what's beyond it. So Narada recites his education, and it's long. The Rig Veda, the Yajur Veda, the Sama Veda, the Atharva as the fourth. The old stories and histories as a fifth Veda. Grammar. The rites for the ancestors. Mathematics. The reading of omens. The keeping of time. Logic. Ethics. The science of the gods, of the sacred word, of spirits, of weapons, of the stars, of serpents. Pretty much the whole library of his world. Then the honest sentence the chapter rests on. With all this, sir, I am only a knower of words, not a knower of the self. I have heard from people like you that the knower of the self crosses beyond sorrow: tarati shokam atmavit. And I am in sorrow, sir. Please take me across. He doesn't say his learning was useless. It's real, and it took a lifetime. It just didn't do the one thing he needed. And Sanatkumara's first answer is startling: everything you've studied is only name. Over the next days he'll lead Narada up a ladder, step by step, from name to something greater, and greater again. Uddalaka taught a proud son who thought he knew. Sanatkumara teaches a humble sage who knows he doesn't.
screen: `TELL ME WHAT YOU KNOW.` · `THE WHOLE LIBRARY OF HIS WORLD.` · `A KNOWER OF WORDS, NOT OF THE SELF.` · `ALL OF IT IS ONLY NAME.` · then, large: `TARATI SHOKAM ATMAVIT.`

segments.voice: List quietly what you know, your skills, your training, the things people come to you for, and let the list be long. Then, as honestly as Narada, notice what none of it has touched, a sorrow, a restlessness, a question, and let it be said, without fixing it, before you rest with the breath.
Atmavit, knower of the self. A sage who knows every subject, admitting he's a knower of words, not of the self, and asking to be taken across sorrow.
Your line: knowledge isn't it. Learning is real; it just isn't the crossing. That's day three hundred fifty-two.

screen: `DAY 352 COUNTS.` → `TOMORROW: NAME, SPEECH, MIND, WILL, THOUGHT.`

howItsDone: Hindu traditions distinguish learning about scripture from knowledge of the self; many teachers quote Narada's confession to students who have studied much and still feel unsettled.

original.note: Sanskrit ātmavit: knower of the self. tarati śokam ātmavit: the knower of the self crosses beyond sorrow.

trapdoor: what you thought: a story about a scholar who learned too much.
what it means: learning is real and good, and still not the same as knowing the self, which is what crosses sorrow.
what a scholar hears: Chandogya 7.1.2–3, Narada's list of sciences, an early catalogue of Vedic learning that counts itihasa-purana as a fifth Veda.

chat.says: Narada knew everything. Why was he still unhappy?
options: He knew words, not the self, and the text says the self-knower crosses sorrow.
He had studied the wrong books, so all his learning was simply useless.
He had forgotten most of what he'd studied, and needed a refresher.
chat.meaning: Narada calls himself a knower of words, not of the self. He has heard that the knower of the self crosses beyond sorrow.

Narada.meaning: a famous sage, learned in every subject of his day

Chandogya.meaning: the Upanishad these lessons come from

sources.ref: Chandogya Upanishad 7.1.1–3 (Narada's learning; the confession; all this is only name)

notes: Narada's list (7.1.2) is long and its terms are rendered variously (rashi = mathematics, daiva = portents, nidhi = chronology, vakovakya = logic, ekayana = ethics/polity, devavidya, brahmavidya, bhutavidya, kshatravidya, nakshatravidya, sarpadevajanavidya). The script gives approximate renderings; confirm.
'Knower of words' renders mantravid (knower of mantras/texts); confirm.
Sanatkumara's opening request ('tell me what you know') per 7.1.1; confirm.

Reviewer changed 'the second great teacher-student dialogue of the Chandogya' to 'another of ... great dialogues' (the Chandogya has several earlier dialogues: Satyakama, Upakosala, the five fires) and the hook's 'miserable' to 'still in sorrow' to match socami (7.1.3).

Title puts "I know the Vedas — I don't know the Self" in quotation marks; it is a summary of 7.1.3, not the text's wording (mantravid evasmi natmavit). Kept because the title is the index head; consider removing the quotation marks in the index.
